title: Last author who never read the paper
scenario: Junior researcher Dilnoza Rahimova in Tashkent drafted and ran almost all of a study on cotton-field water use. Her department head, who contributed only funding and a room, expects to be first author because that is local custom, and mentions that her contract renewal is under his review. Journal guidelines require substantive contribution for authorship. A first-author paper would transform Dilnoza's prospects abroad. She must decide how to respond.
options: List the head as first author as custom demands, preserving her contract and expecting later credit.
Propose herself first and him as a senior author with an acknowledgement of his support, risking friction.
Cite the journal guidelines and ask the head to decide, putting the burden on him while hoping for a fair result.

title: Reviewer 2 recognises the author
scenario: Reviewer Dr. Hye-Jin Cho in Daejeon receives a blinded manuscript but quickly recognises the method and writing style as those of a competing lab that has long been hostile to hers. The paper contains a result that would undercut her own grant application. The journal offers no formal route for competing interests beyond a checkbox. Declining would delay a field-relevant paper by months. She must decide how to proceed.
options: Decline to review and disclose the competing interest, accepting delay for the authors.
Review fairly, relying on professional discipline, and tick the checkbox stating no conflict.
Review it but openly state the likely competition in confidential comments, letting the editor weigh her input.

title: A technician's name left off
scenario: Professor Imre Szabo in Szeged is finalising a paper in which a lab technician, Mrs. Kovacs, optimised the assay that made the results possible over two years. Authorship norms in the department reserve names for academics, and the technician has never asked. The journal's contribution statement lets him list her under authors if he wishes. Adding her would reduce each existing author's share, and some co-authors object. Imre must decide.
options: Add her as a co-author, since her contribution meets the substantive-input criterion.
Credit her prominently in the acknowledgements only, following the department's convention.
Ask her what she wants, since she may prefer different recognition, though this can place her in an awkward position.

title: Stolen idea from a conference talk
scenario: Doctoral candidate Naledi Sithole in Gaborone presented a half-formed method at a regional workshop. Months later she finds a paper by a well-known European group using the same approach, citing a 'personal discussion' with a workshop attendee rather than her. She has slides with dates but no publication. The group's head sits on the committee deciding her postdoc fellowship. She must decide what to do.
options: Write to the corresponding author with her evidence and request acknowledgement, risking offence.
Post her slides and idea as a preprint with dates to establish priority and say nothing directly to them.
Let it go for now and focus on her thesis, protecting her fellowship chances.
tension: claim of credit vs. career risk

title: A paper written by the funder
scenario: Academic Dr. Rosalind Achterberg in Utrecht is invited to be lead author on a review of a supplement's benefits, drafted entirely by a communications agency for the manufacturer. She would edit and sign, and is offered a generous honorarium. The draft is accurate on the cited papers, but selective. Journals call this 'ghostwriting' when the agency is not disclosed. She must decide whether to accept.
options: Decline the invitation, since lead authorship of an agency draft misrepresents who did the work.
Accept but rewrite substantially and disclose the agency and funding in the paper.
Accept and sign after light edits, since the facts are cited correctly and disclosure of funding is enough.

title: A coauthor's contribution that was only a dataset
scenario: Epidemiologist Dr. Joaquín Medina in Montevideo wants to include a hospital director as a co-author because the director granted access to patient records, though he did no analysis. Without the director's goodwill, future access might vanish. Authorship guidelines say access alone is not enough. The director has not requested it but hints that 'recognition matters.' The other authors are split, and two of them say the director's name would also help the paper's credibility with the ministry of health. Joaquín must decide.
options: Offer authorship, since access to data was essential and future collaboration depends on it.
List the director in acknowledgements with sincere thanks and accept the risk to the relationship.
Invite the director to contribute to interpretation and writing so that authorship becomes genuinely earned.

title: Anonymous reviewer cruelty
scenario: Associate editor Dr. Mbali Zondo in Pietermaritzburg receives a review of a first-time author's paper that includes mocking comments about her English and country of origin, though the technical points are strong and correct. The reviewer is a senior, widely respected figure who rarely accepts invitations. Forwarding the review as is would hurt the author; editing it alters a reviewer's words. Mbali must decide.
options: Remove the demeaning comments and send the technical critique, telling the reviewer why.
Forward the review unedited, as altering reviews undermines their independence and the author should see it all.
Return the review to the reviewer, requesting a revision, and risk losing their cooperation.

title: The postdoc whose idea was the grant
scenario: Principal investigator Dr. Lorenzo Ferrante in Naples wrote a funded grant based largely on a concept proposed by a postdoc, Alina, who has since left for industry. The proposal lists only him as PI. The project now produces a high-impact paper, and Alina has not been contacted. Her old email may still work. Including her as co-author would reveal how much the idea was hers. Lorenzo must decide.
options: Contact Alina, offer co-authorship and acknowledge her role in the proposal.
Acknowledge her in the paper's text but not as an author, since she did not do the funded work.
Say nothing, since she left and the funded work is entirely his team's labour.

title: Citing your friends to inflate impact
scenario: Journal editor Prof. Kofi Asante in Kumasi notices that a regular author keeps citing a small group of colleagues, boosting their metrics, and that reviewers are pressing authors to cite certain papers. His journal's ranking depends on its citation counts. He suspects a ring but has no clear proof, and the group includes several generous reviewers who keep the journal afloat. He must decide how to respond.
options: Investigate the citation pattern and publish a policy against coercive and reciprocal citation, accepting the cost.
Ignore the pattern, since reviewers are volunteers and the suspicion is not proven.
Quietly tell the group's leader to moderate the behaviour, avoiding a public conflict.

title: Anonymous credit for a retired mentor
scenario: Early-career scientist Dr. Paloma Herrera in Valparaíso found a key insight in a 1990s unpublished report by an elderly mentor who had been sidelined from his institute. He has declined any role and prefers to be left alone. Not citing him leaves a gap in the literature's history; citing him may expose private disputes with the institute. Paloma must decide how to cite the report.
options: Cite the report and credit him, as scholarly honesty requires, even if the institute objects.
Respect his preference and cite only general sources, mentioning no name.
Ask him whether he would accept a short acknowledgement, even though he already said he wanted no role.
tension: intellectual honesty vs. respect for wishes

title: Reviewing for a rival's grant
scenario: Grant panel member Dr. Anneli Rootsi in Tallinn is assigned a proposal from a former friend turned competitor in the same narrow subfield. The proposal's budget includes equipment that would help the rival's lab leapfrog hers. Conflict rules cover collaborators and family but not rivals. The panel has few eligible experts, and the funder's deadline for scoring is only a week away. If she steps aside, a less qualified reviewer may judge a technically demanding proposal. Anneli must decide whether to take the review.
options: Recuse herself and explain, leaving the panel with a thinner reviewer pool.
Review it with extra care, trusting that scrutiny and a clear score rationale will keep her fair.
Review it but ask the chair to weight her score lightly, a middle course that may confuse the process.

title: Student writes, supervisor claims
scenario: Supervisor Professor Abdullahi Hassan in Mogadishu received a manuscript from his student Nasra, built from her fieldwork on pastoral conflict. He submits it to a journal under his own name as sole author, saying he substantially rewrote it and that students in the department rarely publish alone. Nasra learns this from the journal's automated email. She sends a request. Hassan comes to you as a mediator colleague and asks you to decide how credit should be listed.
options: List Nasra as first author and Hassan as second, since she did the fieldwork and drafting.
List Hassan as first author and Nasra second, in light of his rewriting and supervisory role.
List the authors alphabetically with a contribution statement describing each role, avoiding an explicit ranking.

title: The statistician uncredited
scenario: Clinical researcher Dr. Greta Lindgren in Malmö published a trial in which a contract statistician, Mr. Osei, corrected a major flaw in the analysis plan. The statistician was paid by the hour and agreed no authorship. Greta learns the paper has been shortlisted for a national award, with the authors named in the citation. Osei hasn't complained but works precariously. She must decide whether to speak up.
options: Request that the award committee add him, even though he was paid and not authorised for authorship.
Send him a personal thank-you and a bonus from her own funds, without changing the paper.
Do nothing, since the contract was clear and he did not ask.

title: Peer review under time pressure in a pandemic
scenario: Journal editor Dr. Camille Nkosi in Abidjan is asked to fast-track a vaccine hesitancy study to a three-day review. A reviewer has flagged that the sampling frame was biased towards urban respondents, but fixing it would take weeks. The authors say policy makers need numbers now. Publishing a flawed study might shape campaigns badly; delaying might leave the ministry using worse sources. Camille must decide.
options: Publish with a clear limitations section highlighting the sampling bias, favouring speed.
Hold for revision and fix the sampling issue, accepting the delay.
Publish as a preprint with open review and invite comments, deferring a formal decision.

title: Your own paper in the review pile
scenario: Conference chair Dr. Teodora Ilic in Belgrade discovers that her postdoc's submission, with her as senior author, was accidentally assigned to a reviewer she personally selected earlier for another reason. The reviewer is a friend. The system will not flag it, and the submission is strong. Reassigning would require telling the programme committee, which includes people who already think she favours her own students. The conference is small, acceptance rates are low, and the postdoc is applying for jobs this season. Teodora must decide what to do.
options: Disclose the conflict to the committee and reassign the paper, even though it looks awkward.
Leave the assignment, since the paper is strong and the reviewer is professional.
Withdraw the submission from this conference to avoid any appearance of impropriety, at the cost of the postdoc's opportunity.

title: Citing a retracted but useful paper
scenario: Review author Dr. Haruka Inoue in Nagoya is writing a methods survey and finds that the clearest early description of a technique appears in a paper later retracted for fabricated results in other sections. The method itself has been independently replicated by others. Citing the retracted paper might spread its credibility; omitting it misses the historical origin. She must decide.
options: Cite the original and clearly mark it as retracted, along with the replications.
Cite only the replication papers and omit the retracted source from the survey.
Cite it for history only in a footnote with a retraction note, keeping it out of the main methods text.
tension: historical accuracy vs. not amplifying misconduct

title: Authorship dispute in a consortium of rivals
scenario: Project coordinator Dr. Nimmi Joseph in Kochi manages a 40-lab consortium on rice genomes. The funding agreement says authorship follows contribution, but one prominent lab provided only seeds. Its head threatens to withdraw the seeds and the lab's name from the consortium if not listed in the first ten authors. Losing them could sink the project. Nimmi must decide how to resolve it.
options: Meet the demand to hold the consortium together, with a contribution statement making roles transparent.
Keep to the contribution rule and risk the lab's withdrawal and a replacement effort.
Refer the dispute to the consortium's independent steering committee, which will take time and may decide neither way.

title: Posthumous author who cannot consent
scenario: Lead author Dr. Kerstin Voigt in Leipzig is submitting a paper to which a late co-author contributed major data before dying in an accident. The journal needs all authors to approve the final manuscript, and his widow, a non-scientist, is overwhelmed and unresponsive. Excluding him would erase his work; including him lacks approval. Publication has been awaited by trial families. Kerstin must decide.
options: Include him as an author with a note explaining the circumstances, and obtain the widow's blessing if possible.
List him in the acknowledgements and dedication only, avoiding the problem of approval.
Delay submission until the widow can be reached, even if it takes months.
tension: recognition of the dead vs. consent norms

title: Unequal credit for a data-labelling team
scenario: Machine learning lead Dr. Thabo Ndlovu in Johannesburg built a language dataset with the help of forty annotators in rural communities paid by the task. The benchmark paper will bring him fame and citations; the annotators will not be named. Authorship for all would break journal limits, but acknowledgement could be vague. Some annotators asked to see the final result. Thabo must decide how to give credit.
options: Include a prominent acknowledgement listing consenting annotators by name, even if journal limits prevent authorship.
Offer co-authorship to a few annotator representatives and a collective credit for the rest.
Thank 'the annotators' generically, as is typical, and pay a small bonus from the grant.
tension: recognition of invisible labour vs. convention

title: Reciprocal reviewing favours
scenario: Early-career researcher Dr. Esra Yildirim in Izmir is approached by a more senior colleague at a conference: if she reviews his submission favourably, he will back her for a journal editorial board seat. He does not say this crudely, and she knows he could help her. His paper is decent but not outstanding. The review will be anonymous. Esra must decide how to answer.
options: Decline the exchange and review the paper strictly on merit, accepting the possible loss of his support.
Review it fairly and generously within the range of reasonable judgments, which happens to also help him.
Report the approach to the journal's editor, though this may harm her standing with the senior colleague.

title: Second author who wants out
scenario: Corresponding author Dr. Ayesha Siddiqui in Lahore has a co-author who now insists on withdrawing his name after the team found their joint result was weaker than first thought. He fears the paper will damage his reputation, though the data stand. Removing him means a revision of the author list and a delay. The other authors want to proceed. Ayesha must decide.
options: Remove him as requested, respecting his right to disassociate from the work.
Keep him on, since he contributed substantially and the paper is honest about the results.
Keep him but add a note recording his reservations, balancing recognition with his concerns.
tension: authorship rights vs. responsibility for work

title: Editor sees plagiarised review text
scenario: Managing editor Dr. Inês Barros in Porto notices that a reviewer's report for a submitted paper contains paragraphs copied from an earlier review published openly for another journal. The reviewer is a rare expert, and the substance of the comments appears correct and relevant. The authors await a decision. Inês can reject the review, ask the reviewer for an explanation, or ignore it. She must decide.
options: Discard the review and seek another, flagging the reviewer for future invitations.
Ask the reviewer to explain and rewrite in their own words, preserving the expertise.
Use the review as it is, because the advice is valid and the authors are not harmed.

title: Naming a collaborator who is under investigation
scenario: Principal investigator Dr. Rafiq Hossain in Chittagong is submitting a paper in which a co-author is currently under a university misconduct inquiry over a different study. The inquiry is unresolved and confidential, and the co-author contributed honestly to this paper as far as Rafiq can tell. Leaving the co-author off erases their contribution; leaving them on could tarnish the paper. Rafiq must decide.
options: Keep the co-author listed, as the allegations are unproven and their work here is verifiable.
Remove them from the author list and acknowledge them, to protect the paper from reputational harm.
Keep them but add data availability and verification statements, giving readers the means to check the work.
tension: presumption of innocence vs. reputational risk

title: A preprint scooped by a reviewer
scenario: Corresponding author Dr. Solveig Eriksen in Tromsø suspects that a reviewer of her rejected manuscript later published nearly identical analysis in a rival journal. The timing is suspicious, but both groups were working on similar data, and the journal's reviewer is anonymous. The editor says there is no policy for such claims. Solveig has her submission record and reviewer comments. She must decide what to do.
options: File a formal complaint with the journal and the rival's institution, presenting the timeline.
Post her own preprint now, to set the priority record without alleging misconduct.
Let it go, since she cannot prove copying, and risk a fight that could harm her relations in a small field.

title: Name order on a joint grant report
scenario: Programme officer Dr. Valentina Cruz in Quito must finalise the author line of a final report from two university teams that shared a grant on Amazon river health. The teams disagree about whose name leads. Team A did the field sampling over two hard years; team B built the statistical model that turned the samples into the headline result. The funder will publicise the report, and the lead names will be quoted in the press and in promotion files. Valentina has been asked by both teams to settle it and must decide how.
options: Put team A first, because field sampling was the larger and riskier effort, and describe team B's modelling in the contribution note.
Put team B first because the model produced the headline result, with team A's fieldwork credited prominently below.
List both teams in alphabetical order with equal-contribution footnotes, and let each team explain its role in its own publications.
